'''Kew Gardens''' is a neighborhood in the central area of the [[New York City]] [[Borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]]. Kew Gardens is bounded to the north by the [[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]] and the [[Jackie Robinson Parkway]], to the east by the [[Van Wyck Expressway]] and 131st Street, to the south by [[Hillside Avenue]], and to the west by Park Lane, Abingdon Road, and 118th Street. [[Forest Park (Queens)|Forest Park]] is to the west and the neighborhood of [[Forest Hills, Queens|Forest Hills]] to the northwest, [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park]] north, [[Richmond Hill, Queens|Richmond Hill]] south, [[Briarwood, Queens|Briarwood]] southeast, and [[Kew Gardens Hills, Queens|Kew Gardens Hills]] east.

Kew Gardens is located in [[Queens Community Board 9|Queens Community District 9]] and its ZIP Code is 11415.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 102nd Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 102nd Precinct"/> Politically, Kew Gardens is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 29th District.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf Current City Council Districts for Queens County], [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref> It is located within [[New York's 5th congressional district]].

== History ==
=== Early development ===
Kew Gardens was one of seven planned garden communities built in [[Queens]] from the late 19th century to 1950.<ref name="New York Real Estate: Kew Gardens">[http://www.amny.com/news/local/am-cityliving0828,0,569337,full.story "New York Real Estate: Kew Gardens"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081201134254/http://www.amny.com/news/local/am-cityliving0828,0,569337,full.story |date=December 1, 2008 }}, ''[[AM New York]]'', August 28, 2008. Accessed July 4, 2009.</ref> Much of the area was acquired in 1868 by Englishman Albon P. Man, who developed the neighborhood of [[Richmond Hill, Queens|Hollis Hill]] to the south, chiefly along [[Jamaica Avenue]], while leaving the hilly land to the north undeveloped.<ref name="Thinking">Donovan, Aaron. [https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/15/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-kew-gardens-queens-small-town-feeling-busy-crossroads.html "If You're Thinking of Living In/Kew Gardens, Queens; Small-Town Feeling at a Busy Crossroads"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', October 15, 2000. Accessed August 27, 2018.</ref>

[[Maple Grove Cemetery (Queens)|Maple Grove Cemetery]] on Kew Gardens Road opened in 1875. A [[Long Island Rail Road]] station was built for mourners in October and trains stopped there from mid-November. The station was named Hopedale, after Hopedale Hall, a hotel located at what is now [[Queens Boulevard]] and [[Union Turnpike (New York)|Union Turnpike]]. In the 1890s, the executors of Man's estate laid out the Queens Bridge Golf Course on the hilly terrains south of the railroad. This remained in use until it was bisected in 1908 by the [[Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)|main line]] of the Long Island Rail Road, which had been moved {{convert|600|ft|m}} to the south to eliminate a curve. The golf course was then abandoned and a new station was built in 1909 on Lefferts Boulevard. Man's heirs, Aldrick Man and Albon Man Jr., decided to lay out a new community and called it at first Kew and then Kew Gardens after the well-known [[Kew Gardens|botanical gardens in England]].<ref name="kewname"/> The architects of the development favored English and [[Tudorbethan architecture|neo-Tudor]] styles, which still predominate in many sections of the neighborhood.

=== Urbanization ===
[[File:West Entrance at Maple Grove Cemetery.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.1|Maple Grove Cemetery entrance on Queens Boulevard]]

In 1910, the property was sold piecemeal by the estate and during the next few years streets were extended, land graded and water and sewer pipes installed.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} The first apartment building was the Kew Bolmer at 80{{hyphen}}45 Kew Gardens Road, erected in 1915;<ref>{{cite web | last=Marzlock | first=Ron | title=The Kew Bolmer building | website=Queens Chronicle | date=August 2, 2012 | url=https://www.qchron.com/qboro/i_have_often_walked/the-kew-bolmer-building/article_e8a597cc-3b5d-59c7-8a42-6f84dc5dd43d.html | access-date=June 24, 2024}}</ref> a clubhouse followed in 1916 and a private school, [[The Kew-Forest School|Kew-Forest School]], in 1918. In 1920, the Kew Gardens Inn at the railroad station opened for residential guests, who paid $40 a week for a room and a bath with meals. Elegant one-family houses were built in the 1920s, as were apartment buildings such as Colonial Hall (1921) and Kew Hall (1922) that numbered more than twenty by 1936.

In July 1933, the [[Grand Central Parkway]] opened from the [[Kew Gardens Interchange]] to the edge of [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]].<ref>{{cite web | title=LONG ISLAND ADDS LINKS; Grand Central Parkway And Extension Will Speed Traffic | website=The New York Times | date=July 9, 1933 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1933/07/09/archives/long-island-adds-links-grand-central-parkway-and-extension-will.html | access-date=March 11, 2019}}</ref> Two years later, the [[Jackie Robinson Parkway|Interboro (now Jackie Robinson) Parkway]] was opened, linking Kew Gardens to [[Pennsylvania Avenue (Brooklyn)|Pennsylvania Avenue]] in [[East New York]].<ref>{{cite web | title=OFFICIALS INSPECT NEW CITY HIGHWAY; Park and Bridge Executives See Interborough Parkway, Soon to Be Ready. | website=The New York Times | date=July 12, 1935 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1935/07/12/archives/officials-inspect-new-city-highway-park-and-bridge-executives-see.html | access-date=March 11, 2019}}</ref> Since the parkways used part of the roadbed of Union Turnpike, no houses were demolished.

Around the same time, the construction of the [[IND Queens Boulevard Line|Queens Boulevard subway line]] offered the possibility of quick commutes to the central business district in Midtown Manhattan. ===Later years===
Despite its historical significance, Kew Gardens lacks any landmark protection.<ref name="New York Real Estate: Kew Gardens" />

On November 22, 1950, two [[Long Island Rail Road]] trains [[Kew Gardens train crash|collided in Kew Gardens]]. The trains collided between [[Kew Gardens (LIRR station)|Kew Gardens]] and [[Jamaica (LIRR station)|Jamaica]] stations, killing 78 people and injuring 363. The crash became the worst railway accident in LIRR history, and one of the worst in the history of [[New York (state)|New York]] state.<ref name=RichmondHillHistory>{{cite web | last=Doyle | first=Dennis | title=Long Island Rail Road's Worst Train Crash- The Richmond Hill Historical Society | website=Richmond Hill Historical Society | url=http://www.richmondhillhistory.org/LIRRcrash.html | access-date=September 18, 2018 | archive-date=March 5, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190305081400/http://www.richmondhillhistory.org/LIRRcrash.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1964, the neighborhood gained news notoriety when [[Murder of Kitty Genovese|Kitty Genovese was murdered]] near the [[Kew Gardens (LIRR station)|Kew Gardens]] Long Island Rail Road station. A ''New York Times'' article reported that none of the neighbors responded when she cried for help.<ref>[http://kewgardenshistory.com/ss-nytimes-3.html A Picture History of Kew Gardens, NY – Kitty Genovese – The popular account of the Kitty Genovese murder is mostly wrong as shown by the evidence from her killer's trial and other sources] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090403064713/http://kewgardenshistory.com/ss-nytimes-3.html |date=April 3, 2009 }}</ref> The story came to represent the apathy and anonymity of urban life. The circumstances of the case are disputed to this day. It has been alleged that the critical fact reported by ''[[The New York Times]]'' that "none of the neighbors responded" was false. The case of Kitty Genovese is an oft-cited example of the [[bystander effect]], and the case that originally spurred research on this social psychological phenomenon.<ref>[[Maureen Dowd|Dowd, Maureen]]. [https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/12/nyregion/20-years-after-the-murder-of-kitty-genovese-the-question-remains-why.html "20 Years After The Murder Of Kitty Genovese, The Question Remains: Why?"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', March 12, 1984. Accessed August 27, 2018.</ref>

==Land use==
[[File:House in Kew Gardens 2007.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.1|A typical house in Kew Gardens]]Kew Gardens remains a densely populated residential community, with a mix of one-family homes, apartments, co-ops and others converted and on the way or being converted as condominiums. A new hotel has been completed on 82nd Avenue, reflecting a modernization of the area. However, it is filled mainly with [[apartment]] buildings between four and ten stories high; while many are rentals, some are [[Housing cooperative]]s (co-ops). Although there are no [[New York City Housing Authority]] complexes in Kew Gardens, [[Mitchell-Lama]] buildings provide stabilized rental prices for families or individuals who may need help paying rent. On 83rd Avenue there is a 32-story Mitchell-Lama building. Along the borders of [[Richmond Hill, Queens|Richmond Hill]], [[Briarwood, Queens|Briarwood]], and Jamaica, smaller attached houses exist. Many of these are two or three family homes. Expensive [[single family home]]s are located around the [[Forest Park, Queens|Forest Park]] area. However, many owners are selling out their detached homes to developers who [[Teardown (real estate)|teardown]] and convert them into apartment housing or more expensive, lavish mini-estate houses. This has brought demographic change.

The neighborhood also has many airline personnel because of its proximity to the [[Metropolitan Transportation Authority|MTA]]'s {{NYC bus link|Q10}} bus line to [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]], as well as to [[Delta Air Lines]], [[JetBlue Airways]] and other airlines' special shuttles that serve pilots and flight attendants staying in Kew Gardens.

Kew Gardens's commercial center is Lefferts Boulevard between Austin Street and [[Metropolitan Avenue]]. Major attractions include the Kew Gardens Cinemas, a 1930s art deco movie theater that has been converted into a six-screen multiplex and shows a mix of commercial, independent, and foreign films.<ref>[http://cinematreasures.org/theaters/6156 "Cinema Treasures- Kew Gardens Cinemas"], November 2017. Accessed November 15, 2017.</ref> Lefferts is also home to the only bookstore in central Queens, Kew & Willow Books.<ref>[https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170516/kew-gardens/kew-gardens-bookstore-the-queens-bookshop-81-63-lefferts-blvd "Kew Gardens to Get Its First Bookstore in Decades"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171109194306/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20170516/kew-gardens/kew-gardens-bookstore-the-queens-bookshop-81-63-lefferts-blvd |date=November 9, 2017 }}, May 2017. Accessed May 24, 2017.</ref>

=== Points of interest ===
[[File:KoreanChurchKewGardens.jpg|thumb|upright|right|First Church of Kew Gardens]]
[[Forest Park (Queens)|Forest Park]] is the third-largest park in Queens and is located to the west of Kew Gardens.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_faqs/index.php?action=artikel&cat=1&id=28&artlang=en|title=NYC Parks FAQ}}{{Dead link|date=May 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> The [[Wisconsinan glaciation|Wisconsin Glacier]] retreated from Long Island some 20,000 years ago, leaving behind the hills that now are part of Forest Park.<ref name="NYCPks-ForestPark">{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/forestpark|title=Forest Park : NYC Parks|date=June 26, 1939|website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation|access-date=March 11, 2019}}</ref> The park was home to the Rockaway, Delaware and Lenape Native Americans until Dutch West India Company settlers arrived in 1634 and began establishing towns and pushing the tribes out.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://untappedcities.com/2016/11/02/the-top-10-secrets-of-forest-park-in-queens-nyc/|title=The Top 10 Secrets of Forest Park in Queens, NYC|date=November 2, 2016|work=Untapped Cities|access-date=March 20, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref> The park contains the largest continuous oak forest in Queens.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://untappedcities.com/2016/11/02/the-top-10-secrets-of-forest-park-in-queens-nyc/4/|title=The Top 10 Secrets of Forest Park in Queens, NYC|date=November 2, 2016|work=Untapped Cities|access-date=March 20, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref> Inside the park, the [[Forest Park Carousel]] was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 2004.<ref name="nris2">{{NRISref|version=2010a}}</ref>

In addition to Maple Grove Cemetery, the [[Ralph Johnson Bunche House|Ralph Bunche House]] is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is also a designated [[National Historic Landmark]].<ref name="nris2"/>

The county's civic center, [[Queens Borough Hall]], along with one of the county criminal courts, stand at the northern end of the neighborhood, on Queens Boulevard, in a complex extending from Union Turnpike to Hoover Avenue. ==Demographics==
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Kew Gardens was 23,278, a decrease of 610 (2.6%) from the 23,888 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. Covering an area of {{convert|469.74|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|49.6|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP5">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p5_nta.pdf Table PL-P5 NTA: Total Population and Persons Per Acre - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, February 2012. Accessed June 16, 2016.</ref>

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 49.3% (11,478) [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 6.5% (1,515) [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (37) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 15.6% (3,628) [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (11) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 1.1% (257) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 3.0% (701) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 24.3% (5,651) of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">[http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/data-maps/nyc-population/census2010/t_pl_p3a_nta.pdf Table PL-P3A NTA: Total Population by Mutually Exclusive Race and Hispanic Origin - New York City Neighborhood Tabulation Areas*, 2010], Population Division - [[New York City]] Department of City Planning, March 29, 2011. Accessed June 14, 2016.</ref>

The entirety of Community Board 9, which comprises Kew Gardens, Richmond Hill, and Woodhaven, had 148,465 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 84.3 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-qn9.pdf|title=Kew Gardens and Woodhaven (Including Kew Gardens, Ozone Park, Richmond Hill and Woodhaven)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019|archive-date=August 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190810174431/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-qn9.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is higher than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name=":21">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016-2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017|archive-date=September 9, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170909004755/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}} Most inhabitants are youth and middle-aged adults: 22% are between the ages of between 0–17, 30% between 25–44, and 27% between 45–64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 17% and 7% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|2}}

As of 2017, the median [[household income]] in Community Board 9 was $69,916.<ref name="CB6PUMA">{{cite web|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604111-nyc-queens-community-district-9-richmond-hill-woodhaven-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Queens Community District 9--Richmond Hill & Woodhaven PUMA, NY|publisher=Census Reporter|access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 22% of Kew Gardens and Woodhaven residents lived in poverty, compared to 19% in all of Queens and 20% in all of New York City. One in twelve residents (8%) were unemployed, compared to 8% in Queens and 9% in New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 55% in Kew Gardens and Woodhaven, higher than the boroughwide and citywide rates of 53% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Kew Gardens and Woodhaven are considered to be high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [[gentrification|gentrifying]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|7}}

===Demographic changes===
[[File:Kewgardenssynagogue.jpg|thumb|left|Kew Gardens Synagogue is one of several synagogues and other houses of worship in Kew Gardens, Queens.]]

The Hispanic and Asian populations in Kew Gardens have grown since the [[2000 United States census]]. At the time, the demographics were 66.2% White, 13.0% Asian, 7.0% African American, 0.3% Native American, and 7.4% of other races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 20.0% of the population.<ref>[http://www.zwire.com/site/news.cfm?newsid=19768640&BRD=2731&PAG=461&dept_id=580221&rfi=6 "Kew Gardens—Quiet and Leafy Location"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091004212039/http://www.zwire.com/site/news.cfm?newsid=19768640&BRD=2731&PAG=461&dept_id=580221&rfi=6 |date=October 4, 2009 }}, ''[[Queens Chronicle]]'', June 12, 2008. Accessed July 4, 2009.</ref>

Kew Gardens is ethnically diverse. A large community of [[Jews|Jewish]] refugees from [[Germany]] took shape in the area after the [[Second World War]]  which is reflected still today by the number of active [[synagogue]]s in the area.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/31141678/daily_news/|title=Kew Gardens full of life. Population boost from immigrants|date=September 16, 1999|work=New York Daily News|access-date=May 6, 2019}}</ref> The neighborhood attracted many Chinese immigrants after 1965, about 2,500 [[Iran]]ian Jews arrived after the [[Iranian Revolution]] of 1979,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/31195233/daily_news/|title=Iranian Jews are building new temple in Kew Gardens|last=Danyluk|first=Harry|date=August 11, 1981|work=New York Daily News|access-date=May 6, 2019}}</ref> and immigrants from [[China]], [[Pakistan]], [[Iran]], [[Afghanistan]], [[Israel]], the former [[Soviet Union]], [[India]], [[Bangladesh]] and [[Korea]] settled in Kew Gardens during the 1980s and 1990s. Currently, Kew Gardens has a growing population of [[Bukharian Jews]] from [[Uzbekistan]], alongside a significant [[Orthodox Jewish]] community.<ref name=Thinking/> Also many immigrants from Central America, and South America call Kew Gardens home, as well as immigrants from [[Japan]].

The increase of the Korean population followed the renovation and rededication of the First Church of Kew Gardens, which offers Korean-language services. In recent years, young professionals and Manhattanites looking for greenery, park-like atmosphere and spacious apartments have moved to the area.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}}

Major development in the neighborhood, such as the construction of new apartment complexes and multi-family homes, has resulted in great demographic change as well. Immigrants from [[Latin America]], [[Guyana]], [[South Asia]] and [[East Asia]], and the [[Middle East]] (especially Israel), have moved into these new developments. Even the local cuisine reflects this diversity in Kew Gardens, with [[Russian cuisine|Russian]], [[Italian cuisine|Italian]], [[Indian cuisine|Indian]], [[Pakistani cuisine|Pakistani]], and [[Uzbek cuisine|Uzbek]] dining available to residents and visitors. Many religious groups such as Jews, [[Muslims]], and [[Hindus]], can shop at local markets and [[bazaar]]s that cater to their religious-food needs.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}}

==Police and crime==
Kew Gardens, Richmond Hill, and Woodhaven are patrolled by the 102nd Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 87-34 118th Street.<ref name="NYPD 102nd Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/102nd-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 102nd Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 102nd Precinct ranked 22nd safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/woodhaven/|title=Woodhaven, Richmond Hills, and Kew Gardens – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415053452/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/woodhaven|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 43 per 100,000 people, Kew Gardens and Woodhaven's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is less than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 345 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

The 102nd Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 90.2% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported 2 murders, 24 rapes, 101 robberies, 184 felony assaults, 104 burglaries, 285 grand larcenies, and 99 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-102pct.pdf|title=102nd Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

==Health==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s are more common in Kew Gardens and Woodhaven than in other places citywide, though births to teenage mothers are less common. In Kew Gardens and Woodhaven, there were 92 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 15.7 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Kew Gardens and Woodhaven have a higher than average population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 14%, slightly higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Kew Gardens and Woodhaven is {{convert|0.0073|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, less than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Eleven percent of Kew Gardens and Woodhaven residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is lower than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Kew Gardens and Woodhaven, 23% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 14% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 22% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 22%, 8%, and 23% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 22% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-six percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is about the same as the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 78% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", equal to the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Kew Gardens and Woodhaven, there are 11 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest major hospitals are [[Long Island Jewish Forest Hills]] and [[Jamaica Hospital]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Education ==
Kew Gardens and Woodhaven generally have a lower rate of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 34% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 22% have less than a high school education and 43% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Queens residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Kew Gardens and Woodhaven students excelling in math rose from 34% in 2000 to 61% in 2011, and reading achievement rose from 39% to 48% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_09_11.pdf|title=Kew Gardens / Woodhaven – QN 09|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Kew Gardens and Woodhaven's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is less than the rest of New York City. In Kew Gardens and Woodhaven, 17% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], lower than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}} Additionally, 79% of high school students in Kew Gardens and Woodhaven graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}
